semanticAudit.actionUnmapped: Review the topical plan and assign a crawled URL, or confirm that the topic is still planned.
semanticAudit.actionUnassigned: Review the page in the site structure and assign it manually to the right topic if needed.
semanticAudit.actionStale: Check crawl scope, redirect chain and sitemap; update the assignment only after confirming the target URL.
semanticAudit.actionAmbiguous: Compare intent and SERP role; keep multiple assignments only when intentional.
semanticAudit.actionQuery: Review extracted and full page text; top-40 tokens do not prove a query is absent.
semanticAudit.actionTopic: Verify topic naming and content extraction; do not add a phrase mechanically without context.
semanticAudit.actionLifecycle: Compare the planned stage/date with the editorial state and update the plan manually if needed.
semanticAudit.actionUnhealthy: Open the HTTP responses and redirects; update the assigned URL only after checking the target page.
semanticAudit.actionEntity: Review the full text and declared source; absence from the bounded vocabulary does not verify the fact.
semanticAudit.actionOverlap: Compare page intent and actual SERP/GSC data; lexical similarity alone does not prove cannibalization.
semanticAudit.actionDuplicate: Compare full documents, canonicals and page purpose; hash or SimHash is a review signal, not an automatic merge decision.
semanticAudit.actionOrphan: Check main-content links from other crawled pages and add a contextual link if the page should be discoverable. Navigation, footer and sidebar are intentionally excluded.
semanticAudit.orphanTitle: No inbound link from main content
semanticAudit.orphanDetail: No link from the main content of another crawled page was found in this snapshot. This is not a full site orphan diagnosis: headers, menus, footers, sidebars and out-of-scope pages are excluded.
semanticAudit.topicUnmappedDetail: No URL assigned to this topic was found in the current crawl run. This does not mean the site has no content; only that this snapshot has no confirmation.
semanticAudit.staleTitle: Assignments outside the current crawl run: {{topic}}
semanticAudit.staleDetail: Saved URLs are not present in the selected snapshot. Update the crawl or check whether the page moved.
semanticAudit.lifecycleDetail: The status comes from the user topical plan. Check sources and content before changing it; the crawler does not edit or approve content.
semanticAudit.overdueDetail: The planned publication date is earlier than the audit date. Review the schedule and update the status manually.
semanticAudit.unhealthyTitle: Published topic has a URL outside HTTP 2xx: {{topic}}
semanticAudit.unhealthyDetail: The topical plan declares publication, but at least one assigned URL returned a non-2xx status. Check redirects, URL changes or availability; the crawler does not change publication automatically.
semanticAudit.topicSignalDetail: {{matched}}/{{expected}} topic-name tokens occur in the page top-40 terms ({{percent}}%). This is term visibility lint, not a quality, intent or ranking score.
semanticAudit.pageUnassignedDetail: Manual mapping from page to topical node was not saved. The audit does not assign topics automatically.
semanticAudit.ambiguousDetail: Check whether this is an intentional cross-topic page or two topical nodes that should be separated.
semanticAudit.querySignalDetail: {{matched}}/{{expected}} query tokens occur in the bounded top-40 main-content terms ({{percent}}%). This is a manual-review signal, not relevance or position scoring.
semanticAudit.entityDetail: The declared value is absent from the bounded crawled-content vocabulary. This does not prove it is missing from full page text or that the declaration is wrong.
semanticAudit.duplicateDetail: The crawler computed an identical normalized-content hash.
semanticAudit.similarityDetail: SimHash distance is within the local ≤7/64 threshold. This deterministic comparison is not proof of cannibalization in Google.
semanticAudit.overlapTitle: Review possible URL overlap within one topic
semanticAudit.overlapDetail: Two pages are assigned to the same topical node and share content terms. This is a hypothesis for intent and SERP review, not a keyword-cannibalization verdict.
semanticAudit.actionIntent: Review the query intent evidence and decide whether the editorial intent or topic mapping needs an explicit change.
semanticAudit.intentMismatchTitle: Provider intent differs from the declared topic intent: {{query}}
semanticAudit.intentMismatchDetail: The imported provider intent differs from the topical-node declaration. This is a review signal, not a truth, relevance, ranking or cannibalization verdict.
semanticAudit.actionContentEvidence: Review the full rendered/source content and rerun the crawl if the content region or limits changed.
semanticAudit.contentEvidenceDetail: Semantic lint cannot compare full context because the bounded content evidence is incomplete. Review the rendered/source page manually; this is not a quality or intent verdict.
semanticAudit.contentEvidenceBounded: One or more semantic extraction limits were reached; the evidence is bounded.
semanticAudit.contentEvidenceUnavailable: No primary content region was available.
semanticAudit.contentEvidenceMissingExcerpts: No bounded semantic excerpt was retained.

semanticRunComparison.urlAddedTitle: URL present only in the newer snapshot
semanticRunComparison.urlAddedDetail: The address occurs in the current crawl run but not the baseline. Discovery, scope or crawl limits may explain this; it does not prove a newly published page.
semanticRunComparison.urlMissingTitle: URL not observed in the newer snapshot
semanticRunComparison.urlMissingDetail: The address was in the baseline crawl run but was not found in the current run. This does not prove removal; check scope, robots.txt, limits, errors and redirects.
semanticRunComparison.contentTermsDetail: The comparison covers only the bounded list of terms extracted from main content. Extraction changes do not determine quality or full-text changes.
semanticRunComparison.linkAddedTitle: New internal link observed in content
semanticRunComparison.linkAddedDetail: The edge comes from semantic main-content links, not shared navigation. A snapshot difference is not an automatic linking recommendation.
semanticRunComparison.linkMissingTitle: Internal link not observed in newer content
semanticRunComparison.linkMissingDetail: The link occurred in previously extracted content links but not current links. Missing an edge does not prove removal from the full document.
semanticRunComparison.topicEdgeAddedDetail: This lexical relation is derived from shared main-content terms; it is not a crawled hyperlink or a ranking signal.
semanticRunComparison.topicEdgeMissingTitle: Semantic topic relation not observed in newer content
semanticRunComparison.topicEdgeMissingDetail: The lexical relation occurred in the baseline graph but not the current bounded snapshot. This does not prove that the full content no longer relates.
semanticRunComparison.topicCoverageDetail: The comparison checks only manually assigned URLs for this topical node and their presence in both crawl snapshots.
semanticRunComparison.queryDetail: This is a lexical comparison of bounded main-content terms on assigned URLs. It does not measure SERP visibility, intent or ranking.

Each query stores up to 5 values of 1,000 characters per URL, with a shared 64,000-character limit per run. Selected values are persisted in project data. CSS and bounded XPath queries use the parsed DOM; Regex matches the decoded HTML source and returns the first capture group when present. XPath supports / and // paths, attribute predicates, contains(@attr, …), starts-with(@attr, …), not(@attr), @attr!=…, contains(text(), …), contains(., …), text()='…', positions, and terminal /text() or /@attr; unsupported syntax is reported as an error.

recs.crawlMissingLanguage: Add a valid lang attribute to the <html> element, for example lang="en".
recs.htmlDoctype: Start the document with <!doctype html> exactly once.
recs.htmlMetaCharset: Declare <meta charset="utf-8"> in the first 1024 bytes of the head.
recs.htmlDuplicateId: Make every id attribute unique within the document.
recs.htmlUriInvalid: Fix the URL so it is correctly percent-encoded and resolvable.
recs.missingTitle: Add a unique, descriptive <title> of 30 to 60 characters.
recs.multipleTitle: Keep exactly one <title> element in the head.
recs.titleLength: Rewrite the <title> to 30-60 characters that describe the page.
recs.duplicateTitle: Give every page its own unique title that matches its topic.
recs.missingMetaDescription: Add a unique meta description of 70-160 characters.
recs.metaDescriptionLength: Rewrite the meta description to 70-160 characters.
recs.emptyDescription: Fill in the meta description or remove the empty tag.
recs.multipleMetaDescription: Keep a single meta description tag in the head.
recs.duplicateMetaDescription: Write a unique meta description for every page.
recs.missingCanonical: Add <link rel="canonical"> pointing to the preferred URL of the page.
recs.canonicalTargetReturned: Point the canonical to a URL that answers with HTTP 200.
recs.canonicalAndNoindex: Remove either the canonical or the noindex so the indexing signal is clear.
recs.canonicalDeclarationHas: Use an absolute http(s) URL in the canonical link.
recs.crawlMultipleCanonical: Declare exactly one canonical URL per page.
recs.crawlCanonical: Check that the canonical target is the page you want indexed; make it self-referencing otherwise.
recs.missingH1: Add exactly one <h1> that states the page topic.
recs.multipleH1: Keep a single <h1> and demote the others to <h2>.
recs.heading: Keep headings in order (h1, h2, h3) without skipping levels.
recs.crawlDuplicateContent: Rewrite the page or consolidate duplicates with a canonical or a redirect.
recs.nearDuplicate: Differentiate the content of these pages or merge them.
recs.httpErrorStatus: Fix the server error or remove/redirect links that lead to this URL.
recs.fetchFailed: Check that the server is reachable and answers within the timeout; then re-crawl.
recs.crawlClientRedirect: Replace the meta/JS refresh with a server-side 301 redirect.
recs.redirect: Link directly to the final URL and keep redirect chains to a single hop.
recs.crawlNofollow: Remove nofollow from robots directives unless link equity should really be blocked.
recs.noindex: Remove noindex if the page should appear in search results.
recs.crawlThinContent: Expand the page with useful original content or noindex/merge it.
recs.missingAlt: Add a descriptive alt attribute to every informative image.
recs.jsonldSyntax: Fix the JSON-LD syntax so it parses and validates.
recs.schemaValidation: Reduce the amount of structured data on the page to stay within the limits.
recs.structuredData: Declare every referenced @id in the same graph or remove the reference.
recs.schema: Fix the structured data property reported for this page.
recs.pagination: Make rel=next/prev targets valid, reachable and reciprocal.
recs.ampTarget: Check the AMP page: it must answer 200 and declare the source page as canonical.
recs.nonHtmlResource: No action needed unless this URL should be an HTML page.
recs.responseBody: Reduce the page size or raise the response limit and crawl again.
recs.transientHttpFailure: Check server stability; the request only worked after a retry.
recs.browser: Check the rendering error in the browser console and fix the failing resource.
recs.rendered: Make sure the requested URL does not navigate elsewhere in the browser.
recs.robots: Review the robots.txt rule if this URL should be crawlable.
recs.genericCritical: Fix this problem first: it can prevent the page from being crawled or indexed.
recs.genericWarning: Review the affected pages and correct the reported element.
recs.genericNotice: Optional improvement: review the affected pages when time allows.

healthScore.title: Health score
healthScore.what: A single number from 0 to 100 that sums up how many technical and on-page SEO problems SEOmi found on this one page. 100 means nothing wrong was detected; every problem subtracts points, and serious problems subtract more than small ones.
healthScore.why: Search engines and visitors both prefer pages that load, can be read and are easy to understand. A low score usually means something is blocking the page from ranking, such as a missing title, a broken status code or a noindex tag. The score is a quick triage tool, not a ranking factor that Google reads.
healthScore.action:
Check the colour: 85 and above (green) is healthy, 65 to 84 (amber) needs attention, below 65 (red) needs work now.
Open the issues list further down this screen and start with the Critical items.
Fix one issue, run the audit again and watch the score rise.
Do not chase 100 at any price: a score of 90 with great content beats 100 on a thin page.
healthScore.example: A page with a missing title (Critical), no meta description (Warning) and two images without alt text (Info) might score 68. Adding the title and the description usually brings it above 85.
healthScore.learnMore: The score only covers what SEOmi can measure on this single page. It does not judge your content quality, backlinks or competition.

httpStatus.title: HTTP status code
httpStatus.what: A three-digit answer the web server gives to every request, saying whether the page was delivered. 200 means OK, 301 and 302 mean the page moved, 404 means not found, 410 means gone for good, and 500 or higher means the server itself failed.
httpStatus.why: Google only indexes pages that answer 200 (or follow a redirect to one). A 404 or 5xx page drops out of search results, and visitors see an error. Even a short-lived 500 can make Googlebot visit your site less often.
httpStatus.action:
200: nothing to do, this is correct.
301 or 302: check the final address is the page you want people to land on. Use 301 for permanent moves.
404 or 410: restore the page, or redirect the old address to the closest matching page with a 301.
5xx: ask your hosting provider or developer to check the server logs, then re-run the audit.
After a fix, re-test to confirm the status is now 200.
httpStatus.example: You renamed /blog/seo-tips to /blog/seo-guide and forgot the redirect. The old address now returns 404, so every link and Google result pointing to it leads to an error. A 301 from the old to the new address fixes it.

responseTime.title: Response time
responseTime.what: How many milliseconds (1000 ms = 1 second) the server needed to start sending this page after SEOmi asked for it. It measures the server, not how long the page takes to display in a browser.
responseTime.why: A slow server delays everything that comes after it, so visitors leave and Google crawls fewer of your pages. Google suggests keeping server response under about 200 ms. Above 1000 ms is clearly slow.
responseTime.action:
Under 200 ms: excellent, leave it.
200 to 600 ms: acceptable; consider caching if the page is mostly static.
Above 600 ms: turn on page caching (or a CDN) and compress responses.
Above 1000 ms: check hosting quality, heavy database queries and slow plugins.
Measure two or three times, because a single reading can be a one-off spike.
responseTime.example: A blog post that answers in 1800 ms on shared hosting often drops to 150 to 300 ms after a full-page cache plugin is switched on.

severityCounts.title: Issue severity counts
severityCounts.what: The problems found on this page, grouped by how serious they are. Critical issues can stop the page from ranking or working. Warnings are real weaknesses that cost you traffic or clicks. Info items are small improvements or things worth knowing.
severityCounts.why: Grouping tells you what to fix first. Ten Info items matter less than one Critical, so you avoid spending a day on cosmetic details while a broken canonical tag hides the page from Google.
severityCounts.action:
Fix every Critical issue first, then re-run the audit.
Work through the Warnings, starting with the ones that affect many pages.
Treat Info items as a backlog for when you have time.
A 0 under Critical is the goal, not 0 everywhere.
severityCounts.example: 3 Critical, 5 Warning, 9 Info: start with the 3 Critical ones, for example a missing title, a noindex tag and a 404 on the main image.

wordCount.title: Word count
wordCount.what: The number of words of visible text that SEOmi found in the main content of the page. Menus, scripts and hidden code are not counted. The reading time is estimated at about 200 words per minute.
wordCount.why: Pages with very little text give search engines little to understand, which is called thin content. Long is not automatically better, though: the page must fully answer what the visitor came for.
wordCount.action:
Under 300 words: ask yourself whether the page really answers the question. Add useful detail if not.
300 to 1000 words: normal for most service and product pages.
Over 1500 words: typical for in-depth guides; make sure headings split it into scannable sections.
Compare with the top Google results for your keyword, not with a magic number.
wordCount.example: A product page with 80 words usually loses to competitors who explain materials, sizes, shipping and returns in 400 words.

jsShell.title: Suspected JavaScript shell
jsShell.what: The static HTML of these pages contains almost no text but loads a JavaScript app (for example Next.js or Nuxt). The real content appears only after the browser runs the scripts.
jsShell.why: SEOmi analyses these pages from the raw HTML. Word count, terms, content checks and scores may be too low for them. Text read from a framework payload is shown separately and is not counted as page content.
jsShell.action:
Run the crawl again in rendered (JavaScript) mode to see the content users get.
Check whether search engines get the content without JavaScript (server-side rendering or prerendering).
Treat content scores for these pages with caution.
jsShell.example:
A Next.js page with an empty
and a __NEXT_DATA__ script has 12 words in its static HTML.

titleLength.title: Page title length
titleLength.what: The title is the blue clickable headline in Google results and the text on the browser tab. The length is counted in characters, spaces included.
titleLength.why: Google shows about 50 to 60 characters (roughly 580 pixels). Longer titles are cut off with an ellipsis, so your key words and brand can vanish. Titles that are too short waste a chance to describe the page and attract clicks.
titleLength.action:
Aim for 40 to 65 characters (SEOmi shows green in this range).
Put the main keyword near the start.
Make every page title unique.
Add your brand at the end if it fits, for example after a dash.
Write for people: promise what the visitor will get.
Save and re-audit to see the counter turn green.
titleLength.example: "Cheap shoes" (11 characters) is too short. "Buy Men's Running Shoes Online | Free Returns | ShoeShop" is 53 characters and fits.

metaDescription.title: Meta description
metaDescription.what: A one or two sentence summary of the page, hidden in the code, that Google often shows under the title in search results. It is not visible on the page itself.
metaDescription.why: It does not directly change your ranking, but a clear, inviting description raises the share of people who click your result (click-through rate), which brings more visitors from the same position. When it is missing Google makes up its own snippet, often a random piece of text.
metaDescription.action:
Write a unique description for each page.
Keep it between 120 and 160 characters so it is not cut off.
Include the main keyword naturally, because Google bolds words that match the search.
Say what the visitor gains and add a call to action such as "See prices" or "Learn how".
Do not copy the first paragraph of the page.
metaDescription.example: "Learn how to choose running shoes in 5 steps: fit, cushioning, weight, price and terrain. Includes a free size chart and buying tips." (about 135 characters).

h1Count.title: Number of H1 headings
h1Count.what: H1 is the main heading of a page, the biggest title the visitor sees at the top of the content. It is different from the title tag in the browser tab. Headings H2 to H6 are smaller sub-headings below it.
h1Count.why: The H1 tells visitors and search engines what the page is about in one line. Pages without an H1 look unstructured to screen readers. Several H1s are not an error for Google, but they dilute the message and confuse assistive tools.
h1Count.action:
Exactly one H1 per page is the target.
If there are 0: add one at the top of the content that describes the page, with the main keyword.
If there are 2 or more: keep the best one and change the others to H2 or H3.
Do not use H1 only for styling; use CSS for size instead.
h1Count.example: On a recipe page the H1 is "Easy Homemade Pizza Dough" and the steps below are H2 headings: "Ingredients", "Method", "Tips".

overview.title: Images found
overview.what: How many images SEOmi detected on the page, together with checks on each one: alt text (a short description for people who cannot see the image), size attributes, format and file weight.
overview.why: Images are usually the heaviest part of a page, so they slow it down. Missing alt text hurts blind visitors and removes a chance to appear in Google Images. Missing width and height make the page jump while loading (layout shift).
overview.action:
Give every meaningful image a short, accurate alt text. Use an empty alt for decorative ones.
Set width and height attributes so the browser reserves the space.
Compress photos; try to keep each under 150 KB.
Use modern formats such as WebP or AVIF.
Lazy-load images that are below the first screen.
overview.example: alt="Red running shoe, side view" is useful. alt="image1.jpg" or a stuffed list of keywords is not.

overview.title: Links on the page
overview.what: The count of all links SEOmi found, split into internal (to your own site), external (to other sites) and nofollow (links marked so that search engines do not pass trust through them).
overview.why: Internal links help Google discover pages and understand which ones matter. External links to good sources make content more trustworthy. Broken links frustrate visitors and waste crawl budget.
overview.action:
Check the page links to your important related pages with descriptive text, not "click here".
Fix or remove any link that returns 404.
Link to reputable external sources only; use nofollow for paid or untrusted ones.
Keep the number reasonable: a few dozen on normal pages, not hundreds.
Review security risks, for example links opening a new tab without rel="noopener".
overview.example: A guide about running shoes should link to your "shoe size chart" page with the anchor text "size chart".

theme.title: Theme
theme.what: Chooses how SEOmi looks: Dark, Light, or System, which follows the setting of your computer.
theme.why: It does not change any audit result. Pick what is easiest on your eyes; dark themes reduce glare in dim rooms, light themes are easier to read in bright sunlight, and System switches automatically at night.
theme.action:
Click Dark, Light or System.
The change applies immediately and is remembered next time you open the app.
If you share your screen or print reports, Light is usually easier to read on projectors.
theme.example: Choose System if your computer switches to dark mode in the evening and you want SEOmi to follow.

auditNotifications.title: Audit notifications
auditNotifications.what: When enabled, SEOmi sends a desktop notification as soon as a long audit, crawl or scheduled check finishes, even if the app is in the background.
auditNotifications.why: Large crawls can take minutes or hours. Notifications let you work on something else and come back at the right time. They also tell you about scheduled checks that finished while you were away.
auditNotifications.action:
Turn the switch on if you run crawls or schedules.
When your system asks for permission, choose Allow. If you refused earlier, enable notifications for SEOmi in the system settings.
Turn it off if you find the pop-ups distracting.
The text below the switch shows whether permission was granted.
auditNotifications.example: Start a 5000-page crawl, switch to your email, and get a notification when it is done.

siteFocusScore.title: Site Focus Score (SFS)
siteFocusScore.what: A 0-100 measure of how consistently your pages stay on one core topic. It is a weighted average of the Topical Relevance Score (TRS) of every page: the homepage counts 3x, category and section pages 2x, articles 1x.
siteFocusScore.why: Search engines and readers reward sites that clearly cover one subject. A low SFS means many pages dilute that signal.
siteFocusScore.action:
Read the band: 90-100 excellent, 75-89 good, 60-74 moderate, 40-59 weak, 0-39 critical.
Open the heatmap and fix the lowest pages first.
siteFocusScore.example: A blog about diabetes with 40 articles on diabetes and 8 on travel scores about 80.

topicRelevance.title: Topical Relevance Score (TRS)
topicRelevance.what: A 0-100 score for one URL: how well that page fits the core topic of the site. It combines semantic similarity, keyword overlap and semantic drift.
topicRelevance.why: It shows which individual pages pull the whole site off topic.
topicRelevance.action:
Aim for 75 or more.
Improve pages between 60 and 74.
Remove, redirect or rewrite pages below 40.
topicRelevance.example: A page about glucose meters on a diabetes site: TRS 88. A page about cheap flights: TRS 12.

coreTopicConfidence.title: Core Topic Confidence
coreTopicConfidence.what: How dominant the detected core topic is compared with all other topics found on the site, from 0 to 100 percent.
coreTopicConfidence.why: If the confidence is low, the site has no clear main subject or too few pages were analysed, so scores are less reliable.
coreTopicConfidence.action:
Above 60 percent: trust the topic.
Below that, check the topic label and use the manual override if it is wrong.
coreTopicConfidence.example: If the top topic holds 70 percent of the total term weight, confidence is 70 percent.

onTopicRatio.title: On-topic Ratio
onTopicRatio.what: The share of content pages whose TRS is 60 or higher. Technical pages such as login or cart are not counted.
onTopicRatio.why: It tells you how many pages, not how much weighted score, support the core topic.
onTopicRatio.action: Raise it by fixing borderline pages (40-74) and removing off-topic ones.
onTopicRatio.example: 42 of 50 content pages have TRS 60 or more: the ratio is 84 percent.

semanticSimilarity.title: Semantic Similarity
semanticSimilarity.what: How close the vocabulary of a page is to the core topic profile of the site (cosine similarity, shown as a percentage).
semanticSimilarity.why: It is the largest part of the TRS formula.
semanticSimilarity.action:
80-100 percent is strong, 50-79 moderate, under 50 weak.
Add terms and sections that belong to the core topic.
semanticSimilarity.example: A page on insulin pumps next to a diabetes core topic: 86 percent.

keywordOverlap.title: Keyword Overlap
keywordOverlap.what: The share of the 30-50 most important core topic keywords that appear on the page.
keywordOverlap.why: A page that skips most core keywords cannot support the topic, even when it is well written.
keywordOverlap.action:
Over 60 percent is strong; under 30 percent is off topic.
Add the missing core keywords where they fit naturally.
keywordOverlap.example: The core set has 40 keywords and the page uses 28: overlap 70 percent.

semanticDrift.title: Semantic Drift
semanticDrift.what: The share of the page term weight that belongs to foreign topics, not to the core topic.
semanticDrift.why: High drift means the page spends its words on something else.
semanticDrift.action:
Drift above 50 percent is a red flag.
Cut or move the foreign sections, or split them to their own site area.
semanticDrift.example: A diabetes page with long paragraphs on holiday offers: drift 55 percent.

keywordAlignment.title: Keyword Alignment
keywordAlignment.what: Shows how each frequent keyword of the page relates to the core topic. Symbols: a check mark above 70 percent relevance, a tilde from 40 to 70 percent, a cross below 40 percent.
keywordAlignment.why: It makes visible which words on the page help the topic and which ones distract.
keywordAlignment.action:
Keep and expand the keywords marked with a check mark.
Reduce or remove words marked with a cross.

deltaScore.title: Delta Score
deltaScore.what: A simulated change of the Site Focus Score if you carry out an action. The simulation recalculates the weighted average with the new page values.
deltaScore.why: It lets you rank actions by gain per effort instead of guessing.
deltaScore.action:
Start with actions that have the highest gain and the lowest effort.
Re-crawl after the work to confirm the real gain.

lowConfidence.title: Low confidence
lowConfidence.what: Shown when too few pages were analysed or no topic clearly leads, so the detected core topic may be wrong.
lowConfidence.why: With a small sample one unusual page can change the whole result.
lowConfidence.action:
Crawl more pages.
Check the topic label and override it when it is wrong.
Treat removal advice with caution.
lowConfidence.example: A crawl of 6 pages gives a rough picture only.

benchmark.title: Competitive benchmark
benchmark.what: Your Site Focus Score placed next to the sites that rank in search for your Core Topic. Each competitor is crawled on a small sample of pages and scored with the same formula as your site.
benchmark.why: A score only means something against a reference. Seeing how focused the leaders are tells you how much room you have and what a realistic goal looks like.
benchmark.action:
Run the benchmark with a search results source connected.
Compare your on-topic share and off-topic pages with the top 3.
Open the gaps list and plan content for terms most competitors use.
benchmark.example: If the top 3 average 82 and you have 64, aim at 80 first by fixing your off-topic pages.
benchmark.learnMore: Competitor numbers come from a limited crawl sample, so treat small differences as noise.

benchmarkTarget.title: Target score
benchmarkTarget.what: A suggested goal: at least 80, or the average of the top 3 competitors when they score higher.
benchmarkTarget.why: It turns the comparison into one number to work toward.
benchmarkTarget.action:
Use it as a planning goal.
Re-run the benchmark after your fixes to see the change.

indexGate.title: Indexability gate
indexGate.what: Pages that are noindex or whose canonical points to another URL are left out of the score, so the score reflects pages that can rank.
indexGate.why: Counting pages Google will not index lowers the score and can lead to advice to noindex pages that are already noindex.
indexGate.action:
Check the skipped count.
Fix conflicts listed below the score, such as a noindex pillar.
Use "Include them" only to see the score with all pages.
indexGate.example: A noindex tag page is skipped, not scored as off-topic.

protection.title: URL protection
protection.what: For pages with low topical relevance, shows whether real clicks, conversions, revenue or referring domains argue for keeping them.
protection.why: A low score alone is no reason to delete, redirect or noindex a page that earns traffic or links.
protection.action:
Connect GSC and GA4 so data can be measured.
Treat "Needs data" as unknown, not zero.
Decide by hand; a 301 needs a relevant target.
protection.example: A page with TRS 30 and 80 clicks in 90 days is protected.

tas.title: Topical Authority Score
tas.what: A 0-100 score of how completely, deeply and coherently the site covers its Core Topic compared with the market. It combines topic coverage (35%), entity depth (30%), silo cohesion (25%) and freshness (10%), then scales the result by your Site Focus Score.
tas.why: SFS only measures purity. A site with three perfect articles scores a high SFS yet has almost no authority, because it covers a sliver of the field. TAS measures how much of the field you cover.
tas.action: Aim for 80+ on both SFS and TAS. Low TAS with high SFS: add content. High TAS with low SFS: prune or split off-topic sections. Start with the top item in the expansion plan.

tcr.title: Topic coverage (TCR)
tcr.what: The share of the market’s sub-topics your site covers with a dedicated, on-topic page. Each sub-topic counts by its importance; a close match counts fully, a partial match counts half.
tcr.why: Search engines treat sites that answer the whole range of questions in a field as references. Gaps send visitors, and ranking signals, to competitors.
tcr.action: Above 80%: full authority. Below 40%: fragmentary knowledge. Open the coverage map, filter gaps and publish the most important missing sub-topics first.

esd.title: Entity depth
esd.what: Checks whether a page really covers its sub-topic: the named concepts and attributes the leading pages use, the user questions it answers under their own headings, and how much original material it adds.
esd.why: A long article that misses the key concepts of its field loses to shorter but more complete sources. Length alone does not count.
esd.action: Open a shallow sub-topic: add the missing entities and attributes, answer the listed questions under their own H2 and add data or a table that competitors lack.

scs.title: Silo cohesion
scs.what: Measures how well articles of one theme are tied together by internal links: a pillar page linked both ways with its articles, descriptive anchor texts, no orphan pages and no links from expert pages to off-topic ones.
scs.why: Orphan pages neither pass nor receive topical authority. “Click here” anchors say nothing, so they count only a tenth.
scs.action: Link each orphan from its pillar and related articles, use anchors that describe the target (“diabetic neuropathy symptoms”) and drop links to off-topic pages.

matrix.title: SFS × TAS matrix
matrix.what: Places the site by purity (SFS, horizontal) and completeness (TAS, vertical). The four quadrants are dominant authority, boutique specialist, diluted giant and unfocused generalist.
matrix.why: Why do you have high focus but low authority? Five perfect articles on diabetes give SFS 95 but TAS 14: nothing off-topic, yet 90% of the field is missing.
matrix.action: Keep SFS above 80 while you add new clusters to raise TAS above 80. The highlighted quadrant tells you whether to expand, prune or restructure.

cannibalization.title: Semantic cannibalization
cannibalization.what: Two or more of your pages answer the same search intent: their content and headings are almost identical (cosine similarity from 88%), or both fully cover one reference sub-topic.
cannibalization.why: Internal link signals and relevance are split between the duplicates, so none of them reaches the top positions.
cannibalization.action: Keep the strongest page, move the unique sections into it, 301-redirect the others and update internal links. Use the draft checker before publishing to avoid new overlaps.

aioReadiness.title: AI readiness score (AIO-R)
aioReadiness.what: A 0-100 measure of how easily AI answer engines (Google AI Overviews, Perplexity, Copilot) can lift and quote passages of your pages. It combines self-contained passages (45%), fact density (35%) and extractable structure (20%).
aioReadiness.why: AI engines cut pages into chunks and quote only the chunk that answers the question. Vague or dependent passages are skipped.
aioReadiness.action:
Open the weakest passages and fix the listed problems.
Rewrite them answer-first with explicit names and numbers.
aioReadiness.example: A section titled 'What is a normal blood sugar?' that opens with 'This depends on many factors' scores low.

selfContainment.title: Self-containment
selfContainment.what: Whether a passage still makes sense when cut out of the page: it names its subject and does not start with 'it', 'this' or 'as mentioned above'.
selfContainment.why: A chunk is indexed alone. A dangling pronoun leaves the model without the subject, so the chunk matches fewer questions.
selfContainment.action:
Replace 'it' and 'this' at the start of paragraphs with the real name.
Put the answer in the first 40-60 words under each heading.
selfContainment.example: 'This value should stay under 140.' becomes 'Post-meal blood glucose should stay under 140 mg/dl.'

spoDensity.title: Fact density
spoDensity.what: How many clear subject-predicate-object facts the text states per 100 words, such as 'Fasting glucose is 70-99 mg/dl'. The target is about 3 per 100 words.
spoDensity.why: Models quote verifiable statements. Filler text gives them nothing to extract.
spoDensity.action:
Turn vague sentences into statements with a subject, a verb and a value.
Add units and numbers where you have them.
spoDensity.example: 'Many factors matter' has no fact. 'HbA1c below 7% is the usual treatment target' has one.

extractability.title: Extractability
extractability.what: Whether the page uses structures that parsers lift easily: tables, numbered lists, definition lists and a clear H2/H3 outline.
extractability.why: Generative engines prefer to build answers from tables and step lists because their meaning is explicit.
extractability.action:
Present comparisons as a table and procedures as a numbered list.
Use H2/H3 headings phrased as the questions people ask.
extractability.example: A step-by-step guide written as one long paragraph scores lower than the same guide as an ordered list.

answerFirst.title: Answer-first
answerFirst.what: The first 40-60 words under a heading should answer the heading directly, naming the subject and giving a fact.
answerFirst.why: RAG retrieval compares the question with the start of the chunk. A long preamble lowers the match.
answerFirst.action:
Write the direct answer first, then the context.
Repeat the heading's key term in the opening sentence.
answerFirst.example: Heading 'How long does a CGM sensor last?' followed by 'A CGM sensor lasts 10-15 days, depending on the model.'

chunking.title: Chunking simulation
chunking.what: SEOmi cuts every page the way a RAG index does: one chunk per H2/H3 section, long sections split into windows of about 300 tokens.
chunking.why: You see the page as the retrieval system sees it: a set of separate passages, each judged on its own.
chunking.action:
Check the chunk score of each weak passage.
Keep sections short enough to be one chunk.
chunking.example: A 900-token section becomes about three chunks; only the first one sits directly under the heading.

trustScore.title: Entity Trust Score
trustScore.what: A 0-100 score of how well search engines can verify who publishes and writes your content. It averages four layers: entity graph, author topic fit, source quality and editorial transparency.
trustScore.why: For health, finance and legal topics, strong topical focus is not enough. Pages without a verifiable author and publisher rarely reach the top results.
trustScore.action:
Read the critical items in the list first.
Fix the lowest layer, then re-crawl to see the score move.

schemaGraph.title: Entity graph (JSON-LD)
schemaGraph.what: Checks that your structured data names the publisher and each author as entities with a stable @id and sameAs links, and that articles carry author, dates, reviewer and citations.
schemaGraph.why: Linked entities let search engines match your authors to known people and organizations instead of guessing from plain text.
schemaGraph.action:
Add Organization and Person markup with @id.
Link each person and the publisher to Wikidata, ORCID, LinkedIn or an official register with sameAs.
Use the JSON-LD generator below the author list.

authorAlignment.title: Author topic fit
authorAlignment.what: Compares each author's declared expertise (job title, knowsAbout and profile page) with the core topic of the site.
authorAlignment.why: An article on insulin therapy signed by a marketing copywriter is a weak expertise signal.
authorAlignment.action:
Assign articles to authors whose profile matches the topic.
Add jobTitle and knowsAbout to the Person markup.
Publish a profile page for every author.

citationQuality.title: Source quality
citationQuality.what: Shows how many article pages link out to trusted sources such as .gov, .edu, PubMed, NCBI, WHO or scientific publishers, and how many outbound links are broken.
citationQuality.why: Citing primary sources shows that claims are verifiable. Dead references weaken that signal.
citationQuality.action:
Add references to primary sources in each expert article.
Replace or remove broken outbound links.
Check external links in the Links tab to refresh status codes.

transparency.title: Editorial transparency
transparency.what: Looks for an editorial policy, an About page, a contact page, company registry data and visible modified or review dates on articles.
transparency.why: Readers and search engines need to know who is behind the site and how content is checked.
transparency.action:
Publish an editorial and fact-checking policy.
Add contact details and company registry data.
Show the last update date on every article.

ymyl.title: YMYL topics
ymyl.what: Your Money or Your Life: subjects such as health, finance and law, where wrong information can harm readers.
ymyl.why: Search quality guidelines apply the highest trust requirements to these topics, so missing authors or reviewers count as critical gaps.
ymyl.action:
Name a qualified author on every article.
Add a reviewer with credentials for medical or legal content.
Cite primary sources.

sameAs.title: sameAs links
sameAs.what: A schema.org property that points from a person or organization to the same entity elsewhere: Wikidata, ORCID, LinkedIn or an official register.
sameAs.why: It lets search engines confirm that your author is the real person with those credentials.
sameAs.action:
Add at least one authoritative sameAs URL per author and for the publisher.
Use the same name and spelling as on that profile.

bus.title: Link quarantine
bus.what: URLs that another module wants to remove or redirect with a 301 are kept out of every link recommendation.
bus.why: Without it one panel tells you to link to a page another panel tells you to delete.
bus.action:
Review the list.
Resolve any conflict shown in red before you deploy.

brief.title: 1-click brief
brief.what: Creates or updates the content brief for this page from the data of the module that made the recommendation.
brief.why: The brief starts with the real missing entities, links, questions and sources instead of copied text.
brief.action:
Click the button.
Open the Brief Workstation and edit the draft.
Click again later to refresh the data without creating a duplicate.

deploy.title: Deployment artifacts
deploy.what: Ready rule files for redirects and removals: Apache, Nginx, Cloudflare Bulk Redirects and WordPress Redirection.
deploy.why: Rules are checked for loops and chains first, so you do not ship a redirect that breaks crawling.
deploy.action:
Download the file for your server.
Deploy it on a staging copy first.
Mark the task as implemented and verify on the next crawl.

tasks.title: Task tracker
tasks.what: Keeps each recommended change as a task: planned, implemented, then verified or failed.
tasks.why: The next crawl checks the real result and shows how the module score changed since the baseline.
tasks.action:
Add a task from a recommendation.
Mark it implemented after you deploy.
Run a new crawl and click Verify.

sla.title: Owner and SLA
sla.what: Who is responsible for the task, how urgent it is and the date it must be done.
sla.why: Tasks with an owner and a date do not get lost, and overdue ones are easy to filter.
sla.action:
Type the owner name.
Pick the priority and the SLA date.
Use the filters to see your tasks or the overdue ones.

panel.title: Semantic PageRank
panel.what: Internal PageRank (damping 0.85) scaled to 0-100, with flags for pages that pass no links, receive too few, or send most links to unrelated pages.
panel.why: It shows where link authority pools or drains inside your own site.
panel.action:
Add outgoing links to dead ends.
Link to under-linked pages from strong related pages.
Review leaks.

radar.title: Semantic Decay Radar
radar.what: Compares saved SERP snapshots of the same query, market, provider and model: centroid shift, new or lost consensus entities, intent and format changes.
radar.why: The top results can drift away from your page long before rankings drop.
radar.action:
Open the cited URLs.
Decide manually whether to refresh the page.

panel.title: Search intent (SIJA)
panel.what: Classifies the page into one of 8 micro-intents from its structure (tables, lists, forms, product cards) and compares it with the average of the real TOP 5 pages.
panel.why: A page whose format differs from what the SERP shows often ranks poorly for that query.
panel.action:
Open the TOP pages.
Add the missing format, such as a table or a tool.
Treat this as a hint, not a verdict.

check.title: Pre-publish check
check.what: Simulates adding this draft to your site: change in Site Focus Score, similarity to existing pages and whether each passage works on its own.
check.why: It catches a duplicate or off-topic page before it goes live.
check.action:
Fix every listed reason.
Re-run the check.
Publish only after your own review.

hreflang.title: International parity
hreflang.what: Compares topic depth across the language versions linked by hreflang with a reference language, and marks each topic covered, shallow, missing or intentionally local.
hreflang.why: It separates a real content gap from a market that deliberately offers something different.
hreflang.action:
Check the missing and shallow topics.
Mark topics a market does not need as local.
The tool never changes hreflang for you.

tbva.title: Off-page topical authority
tbva.what: Adds up the provider authority of follow backlinks, weighted by how close each source page is to your topic. Also finds paragraphs that mention your brand and your core entity together.
tbva.why: A few relevant links can matter more than many unrelated ones.
tbva.action:
Review the sources with low similarity.
Look at unlinked mentions as outreach leads.
Read negated mentions yourself.

costGate.title: LLM cost and fact gate
costGate.what: Counts what AI calls cost and what the cache and local models saved. Medical and financial sentences with a dose or amount missing from the source are rejected.
costGate.why: Remote providers cost money and receive your page text. Invented doses in health or finance content are dangerous.
costGate.action:
Prefer a local model for big batches.
Check rejected sentences against the source.
Approve YMYL text yourself before it reaches the CMS.

informationGain.title: Template Information Gain
informationGain.what: Share of each page that is not boilerplate shared with the other pages built from the same template. Low gain means thousands of near-copies.
informationGain.why: Google can filter a whole template segment as thin content. One template warning is easier to fix than thousands of page warnings.
informationGain.action:
Add unique data to each page (local facts, numbers, reviews).
Or noindex the segment until it has real content.
Re-crawl and check that the gain rises.

gapDomains.title: Outreach targets
gapDomains.what: Sites that link to your TOP3 competitors but not to you, ranked by how many competitors they link to and by their authority.
gapDomains.why: A site that already links to several competitors is the warmest place to ask for a link, as long as you bring something new.
gapDomains.action:
Start from the top of the list.
Open the draft, add a source only you can offer, and edit it.
Send it yourself from your own mailbox. SEOmi never sends anything.

updateWindow.title: Google update window
updateWindow.what: Days when Google rolled out an update or the whole market was unusually volatile. The result is shown with an uncertainty range and flagged when the period overlaps such a window.
updateWindow.why: A control group on the same site suffers from an update just like the test group, so a drop or gain can be the market and not your change.
updateWindow.action:
Treat a flagged result as inconclusive.
Wait until the update window ends and compare again.
Use an external market baseline when you have one.

score.title: IGOS score
score.what: Information gain over what the real TOP results already say: new on-topic entities, evidence density, experience markers and subtopic spread, reduced when the baseline is thin.
score.why: It shows what your page adds beyond the consensus. Markers only show declared experience; they do not prove research or originality.
score.action:
Check the four components.
Add the missing fundamentals.
Re-run after editing.

heatmap.title: Paragraph heatmap
heatmap.what: Each paragraph is labelled Echo (close copy of a competitor passage), Gain (on-topic and new), Drift (off-topic) or Neutral.
heatmap.why: Echo adds nothing new and drift dilutes the topic. Labels use text, not only colour.
heatmap.action:
Open Echo and Drift paragraphs first.
Use arrow keys to move between paragraphs.
Rewrite or refocus them.

coverage.title: Baseline coverage
coverage.what: Share of consensus entities your page already covers. Below 50% the score is multiplied by a penalty.
coverage.why: Without the common foundation a page with some novelty still does not match the topic.
coverage.action:
Cover the missing consensus entities.
Then add the new facts.

drawer.title: How the Site Focus Score works
drawer.weightCategory: Categories, sections, pillar and hub pages: weight 2
drawer.sfsFormula: SFS = sum(weight x TRS) / sum(weight), over all analysed pages
drawer.trsFormula: TRS = clamp(0..100, (0.5 x Similarity + 0.3 x Overlap - 0.2 x Drift) x 125)
drawer.trsLexical: Without the semantic component: TRS = clamp(0..100, (0.75 x Overlap - 0.25 x LexicalDrift) x 125)
drawer.bands: Bands: 90-100 excellent, 75-89 good, 60-74 moderate, 40-59 weak, 0-39 critical.
drawer.onTopic: A page counts as on topic from TRS 60.

reasons.incomparable-scope: The nearest periods have different properties or filters, or do not cover the URL.
reasons.period-length-mismatch: Period lengths differ by more than 10%.
reasons.rows-truncated: Saved page rows are truncated; the page comparison may be incomplete.
reasons.low-volume: Baseline clicks are below 30; the volume is too low for a reliable comparison.
reasons.pending: The intervention date is in the future; evaluation is pending.

linkInjector.title: Contextual link injector
linkInjector.description: Top 10 links to add: the donor's H2/H3 section with the most shared terms, a ready sentence in the page's language and the target's SPRS change from the link-graph solver. Quarantined pages are excluded. The SPRS change is a model estimate, not a ranking or traffic forecast.
linkInjector.empty: No candidate has a donor H2/H3 section that mentions the shared terms.
linkInjector.gain: Expected SPRS change of the target: {{value}} (0–100 scale)
linkInjector.gainUnknown: Expected SPRS change: unknown (page outside the solver graph)
linkInjector.languageFallback: Page language unknown: the sentence is in English.

offPageLinksUi.profileSummary: {{raw}} raw links from {{domains}} source domains ({{follow}} with a follow link). Sitewide domains: {{sitewide}} ({{share}}% of raw links); repeated domains: {{repeated}}. TBVA counts one link per source domain.
offPageLinksUi.sample: Based on the loaded sample, not the full provider profile.
offPageLinksUi.complete: Based on all rows the provider returned.
offPageLinksUi.rule: Sitewide = at least 5 source pages with at most 2 distinct anchors (uncalibrated heuristic, not a penalty).
offPageLinksUi.anchorNote: Searches the provider-reported anchor text in the fetched source text. The text has no link markup, so a match shows the surrounding words, not proof that this occurrence is the link.
offPageLinksUi.noAnchors: No analysed source page has a link in the loaded sample.

status.not-found: anchor not found in the source text
status.no-anchor-text: no anchor text (for example an image link)

imagePhashUi.title: Near-duplicate images (perceptual hash)
imagePhashUi.note: Downloads up to {{max}} of the site's own images once, in this app, and compares their 64-bit perceptual hashes. Images whose server blocks cross-origin reads stay unavailable. A match means the pictures look alike; it does not show stock use, authorship or lack of value.
imagePhashUi.uncalibrated: Default 8 bits; this threshold is not calibrated on real data.
imagePhashUi.noPairs: No near-duplicate pair at this threshold.
imagePhashUi.external: Comparison with external image search results: unavailable (no images provider configured).

causalImpactUi.title: Counterfactual estimate (control series)
causalImpactUi.method: Daily Search Console clicks of this property are regressed on an independent control property over up to 90 days before the change; the model predicts the clicks without the change. Frequentist approximation of Causal Impact, without seasonality modelling.

unavailable.page-series-unavailable: Not estimable for a single URL: only property-level daily clicks are saved.
unavailable.no-test-series: Not estimable: no saved daily Search Console series for this site.

status.estimated: Estimated from {{pre}} pre-period and {{post}} post-period days.
status.not-estimable: Not estimable ({{pre}} pre-period and {{post}} post-period days with data).

reasons.missing-data: More than 10% of days are missing in a window.
reasons.no-control: No independent control property with the same filters is saved. Save Search Console data for another domain to use as a control.
reasons.flat-control: The control series has no variation in the pre-period.
reasons.poor-prefit: The control explains too little of the pre-period (R² below 0.5).
reasons.placebo-failed: A placebo test inside the pre-period found an effect where none should be; the model is unreliable.

causalImpactUi.placeboPassed: Placebo test passed (pre-period interval {{lower}} to {{upper}} includes zero).
causalImpactUi.placeboFailed: Placebo test failed (pre-period interval {{lower}} to {{upper}} excludes zero).
causalImpactUi.absolute: Cumulative effect on clicks: {{value}} (95% interval {{lower}} to {{upper}}).
causalImpactUi.probability: Probability that the effect has this sign: {{value}} (normal approximation, not a Bayesian posterior).
causalImpactUi.caveat: An estimate adjusted for the control is not proof of causality. Other changes, Google updates or a shift that also affects the control can bias it. No ROI is inferred.

revenueImportUi.title: Revenue (optional GA4 export)
revenueImportUi.model: Import a GA4 report CSV with landing page and revenue, filtered to organic search sessions. Revenue is attributed to the session landing page as GA4 reports it and kept in the currency you state. Pages missing from the export stay unknown, not zero.
revenueImportUi.none: No revenue export imported; revenue stays unavailable.
revenueImportUi.organic: The export contains organic search sessions only

errors.invalid-currency: Enter the property currency as a 3-letter ISO code, for example EUR.
errors.not-organic: Confirm that the export is limited to organic search sessions.
errors.no-header: No header with a landing page column and a revenue column was found.
errors.no-rows: The file has no landing page with a numeric revenue value.
errors.storage-failed: Local storage could not be updated; the import was not saved.
